# 3.1 Overview of the Financial System: Key file (for the AI tutor only)

## Lesson facts relevant to the questions

- The learner has studied the time value of money (Lesson 0.1, "Compounding and the Time Value of Money" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/0-1-time-value-of-money/), variance, standard deviation and diversification (Lesson 0.3, "Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/0-3-probability/), adverse selection and moral hazard (Lesson 1.9, "Information Economics" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/1-9-information-economics/), and banks, runs and deposit insurance (Lesson 2.3, "Money and Banking" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/2-3-money-banking/). Percentage calculations are in percentage points.
- The lesson: functions of the financial system (moving resources over time, sharing risk, pooling funds, producing information); direct and indirect finance; reasons for intermediaries (diversification, information costs, maturity and liquidity transformation). The money market (up to a year: Treasury bills, commercial paper, repo; money market fund assets about 7.65 trillion dollars in early December 2025, ICI) and the capital market; debt versus equity. Primary market (IPO, underwriting) and secondary market (liquidity, price discovery).
- The lesson: market makers quote bid and ask prices; the spread is the cost of trading immediately and also compensates for adverse selection; US stocks have settled T+1 since May 28, 2024. Short selling: borrow shares, sell them, buy back later; the short seller pays dividends; the potential loss is unlimited. Market, limit and stop orders; the order book and price impact. The order book of Figure 5-1: midpoint 100.00; asks 100.05 × 500, 100.10 × 500, 100.20 × 1000, 100.40 × 2000; bids 99.95 × 500, 99.90 × 800, 99.80 × 1000, 99.60 × 2000; a market-buy size slider from 100 to 4000 in steps of 100, default 500; the readout shows the average price, its percentage above the midpoint and the extra amount paid.

## Check question C1

As long as a bank makes enough loans, its default losses as a share of total lending will be very stable, whether or not the economy falls into recession.

Correct answer: False

Hint (give it after a wrong answer, without the verdict): Think: which kind of risk can more loans diversify away? In a recession, are defaults by different borrowers still independent?

**Reference answer**

False. More loans diversify away only defaults that are independent of each other. In a recession many borrowers get into trouble at the same time, so defaults are positively correlated; this part of the risk cannot be diversified away by making more loans, and the loss share rises noticeably in recessions.

**Common errors**

- Thinking that diversification removes all risk. Loan defaults rise together in recessions, and correlated risk cannot be diversified away by making more loans.

## Check question C2

A stock suddenly attracts many traders who may have inside information. What is the market maker most likely to do?

- (A) Narrow the bid-ask spread to attract more trading
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): A narrower spread makes losses to informed traders harder to recover. With more informed traders, does the market maker face more risk or less?
- (B) Widen the bid-ask spread ← Correct answer
- (C) Keep the spread unchanged, because the spread depends only on trading volume
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): The spread does not depend only on volume; it also compensates the market maker for risk, including the risk of trading with people who know more.
- (D) Quote only a bid and no ask
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): A market maker quotes both a bid and an ask; quoting only one side does not solve the problem of trading with informed traders.

**Reference answer**

(B). Trading with informed traders, the market maker tends to sell just before prices rise and buy just before they fall, and loses money (adverse selection). The more informed traders there are, the wider the spread the market maker needs to recover these losses from other traders.

**Common errors**

- Ignoring trading costs and assuming one can trade at the midpoint or the last trade price. Immediate buys pay the ask, immediate sells get the bid, and large orders also have price impact.

## Check question C3

In Figure 5-1, raise the market buy order from 1500 shares to 3000 shares. Compared with trading at the midpoint, how does the total extra amount paid change?

- (A) It exactly doubles
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): The total doubles exactly only if the extra paid per share stays the same. In the order book, at what prices do the later shares trade?
- (B) It rises, but less than double
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Look at the price levels the second 1500 shares must take, and compare their extra cost per share with the first 1500.
- (C) It more than doubles ← Correct answer
- (D) It does not change
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): With more shares, the prices reached change too, so the total extra amount cannot stay the same.

**Reference answer**

(C). 1500 shares cost about 175 dollars extra and 3000 shares about 675 dollars. The later shares must take higher price levels, so the extra paid per share rises with order size: price impact grows faster than the order.

**Common errors**

- Ignoring trading costs and assuming one can trade at the midpoint or the last trade price. Immediate buys pay the ask, immediate sells get the bid, and large orders also have price impact.

## Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)

Issuing corporate bonds involves a fixed cost of about 1 million dollars (underwriting, legal work, ratings and so on), whatever the amount. A small firm borrowing 5 million dollars usually borrows from a bank, while a large company borrowing 1 billion dollars often issues bonds directly. Apart from the fixed cost, explain with information problems why small firms rely more on banks.

**Reference answer**

The fixed cost is 20% of the small firm's borrowing and only 0.1% of the large company's. Beyond that, investors find it hard to judge a small firm's quality: those willing to pay high rates tend to be riskier borrowers (adverse selection), and after borrowing the firm may take more risk (moral hazard). It does not pay for many dispersed bondholders each to investigate and monitor; a bank can investigate in one place, build information through a long relationship, write covenants into the loan and keep monitoring, solving the information problems at lower cost. Large companies publish information and have ratings, so these problems are much smaller.

**Grading points**

- Explains the bank's advantage with adverse selection, moral hazard and monitoring costs.

**Common errors**

- Thinking that small firms rely on banks only because issuing bonds has a high fixed cost, and missing that banks gain information through long relationships and monitoring, which reduces adverse selection and moral hazard.

## Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)

An investor sells short 100 shares at 50 dollars; while the position is open the company pays a dividend of 1 dollar per share; the shares are then bought back at 60 dollars. (a) What is the gain or loss? (b) Many shares of a stock have been sold short, and then the company announces unexpected good news. Why might the price rise by more than the good news alone is worth? Why can short sellers often not "wait for the price to fall and buy back then"?

**Reference answer**

(a) The sale brings 5000, buying back costs 6000, and the dividend costs 100: a loss of $1000 + 100 = 1100$ dollars.
(b) A short seller's loss grows as the price rises, without limit. When the price rises, the broker asks for more margin and the lender may recall the shares; short sellers who cannot add money or borrow the shares elsewhere must buy back. In a heavily shorted stock these forced purchases push the price up further and force still more short sellers to buy back: a short squeeze. So the price can rise far beyond what the good news is worth. Even a short seller who is right in the end may be forced out at a high price, with a loss, before the price falls.

**Grading points**

- (a) A loss of 1100, including the dividend.
- (b) Explains that margin calls and recalled shares force short sellers to buy back as the price rises, and that these purchases push the price higher (a short squeeze). Saying only that a short seller's loss is unlimited, without the mechanism of forced buybacks: needs revision.

Numeric answers: loss = 1100

**Common errors**

- Forgetting that the short seller pays the dividends; or thinking that a short seller can always wait for the price to fall before buying back, and missing that margin calls and the lender recalling the shares can force a buyback at a high price.

## Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)

A company sells 10 million shares in an IPO at 20 dollars; the first-day closing price is 25 dollars. (a) The chief executive says: "The 25% first-day gain shows the IPO was a great success, and the company benefited from the rise in its share price." Compared with selling at the first-day close, how much less did the company receive? Evaluate the statement. (b) Studies find such first-day gains on average in IPOs. Give one explanation based on asymmetric information between issuers and investors.

**Reference answer**

(a) $10 \times (25 - 20) = 50$ million dollars. The company receives money only when it issues the shares; later trading is between investors (the secondary market), and the gain from the price rise goes to the investors who bought the new shares, not to the company. The larger the first-day gain, the lower the offer price was set and the more money the company "left on the table".
(b) For example: well-informed investors apply only for good IPOs, so less-informed investors get little of the good ones and a lot of the bad ones (the "winner's curse", a form of adverse selection). For them to keep taking part, offer prices must be set lower on average.

**Grading points**

- (a) 50 million dollars, and notes that the gain goes to the buyers of the new shares, not to the company.
- (b) A reasonable explanation based on asymmetric information.

Numeric answers: left = 50

**Common errors**

- Thinking that trading in the secondary market raises money for the company. Only issuance in the primary market does; when the price rises after listing, the issuer does not receive that money.

## Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)

The midpoint is 100.00 and the ask 100.05. You want to buy one share: (i) a market order, filled at 100.05; or (ii) a limit order at 99.98, with an estimated 60% chance of a fill; if not filled, it is usually because the price has risen, and you then buy with a market order at an ask of 100.35.
(a) What is the expected price with the limit order? Which choice is better?
(b) When is a limit order most likely to be filled? Why does this mean limit orders also carry a kind of "adverse selection" cost?

**Reference answer**

(a) $0.6 \times 99.98 + 0.4 \times 100.35 = 100.128$, above 100.05, so here the market order is better.
(b) A limit buy is most likely to fill when the price is falling (someone is eager to sell, or bad news has arrived); when the price is rising, it does not fill. So limit orders tend to buy when it would have been better not to and miss when it would have been better to buy: being filled is itself a sign the price may keep falling.

**Grading points**

- (a) 100.128; the market order is better.
- (b) Explains the link between fills and falling prices.

Numeric answers: e = 100.128

**Common errors**

- Ignoring trading costs and assuming one can trade at the midpoint or the last trade price. Immediate buys pay the ask, immediate sells get the bid, and large orders also have price impact.

## Exercises Question 5 (id: Q5)

Money market funds usually keep their share value at 1.00 dollar. On September 16, 2008, a large US money market fund's share value fell below 1 dollar because Lehman Brothers commercial paper it held defaulted. Suppose a fund loses 3% of its assets but still pays 1.00 dollar to those who redeem first. Why would investors rush to redeem? Compared with bank deposits, what protection did money market funds lack at the time?

**Reference answer**

The assets are worth only 0.97 dollars per share. Those who redeem first take 1.00 and leave the loss to those who remain, who then get less; everyone wants to get out first, so everyone redeems, the fund must sell assets cheaply, and losses grow. As with the bank runs of Lesson 2.3, "Money and Banking" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/2-3-money-banking/, it is a self-fulfilling "first come, first served".
Money market funds then had no deposit insurance and no access to central bank lending; investors treated them as being as safe as deposits, but their value depends on the assets they hold.

**Grading points**

- Explains the first-come-first-served run.
- Notes the lack of deposit insurance and central bank support.

**Common errors**

- Thinking that money market funds are as safe as bank deposits. At the time they had no deposit insurance, their value depended on their assets, and first-come-first-served redemptions at a fixed share value invited runs.
